title: Art School Confidential
full_review:
"Art School Confidential" (United Artists/Sony Classics) has an identity crisis.

The film can't decide if it's a touching coming-of-age story, gross-out frat movie, murder mystery or mordant black comedy.

Director Terry Zwigoff's only fiftully amusing film was adapted by Daniel Clowes from his comic strip, as with the pair's previous "Ghost World."

This one concerns a sensitive art school student Jerome Platz (Max Minghella), who enrolls at the smallish Strathmore Institute.

He chooses the school as much for the attractive artist's model, Audrey (Sophia Myles), on the cover of the brochure as the curriculum, and as he begins his freshman year struggles to find his artistic voice amid loutish classmates, colorful teachers like Professor Sandiford (John Malkovich) and Sophie (Angelica Huston), and an embittered and alcoholic failed artist, Jimmy (Jim Broadbent). All of this plays out against the backdrop of a mysterious rash of strangulation murders on campus.

He indeed meets Audrey, herself the daughter of a famous artist, fairly early in the game, and she treats him kindly, but keeps him at a friendly distance.

Jerome has the perception (and probably the true talent) that most of the others lack, but time and again his paintings are overlooked in favor of the inferior output of his classmates, including blond jock Jonah (Matt Keeslar), whose simplistic work is unaccountably lauded.

"Art School Confidential" does make some sharply satiric points about the art world. (Jerome, in desperation, must resort to imitation, then plagiarism, to make his mark, though there are dire consequences.) The politics of artistic success are well illustrated, as in the jockeying for position with restaurateur Broadway Bob, played by an unbilled Steve Buscemi, who allows promising students wall space in his establishment.

But the overall tone of the film is fairly raunchy, courtesy of Jerome's roommate Vince (Ethan Suplee), a foul-mouthed would-be filmmaker, and his dopey friend Bardo (Joel David Moore), who try to jump-start their friend's love life, resulting in an uneasy mixture of adolescent angst and "40-Year-Old Virgin" crudeness.

The coarse language (and the two extended scenes of art-class nudity) almost push this into the "O" classification, but there's just enough substance here -- the main themes of a talented artist trying to find himself, and the fraudulence of many elements of the art world -- to justify the still restrictive "L" rating.

The film contains pervasive profanity, rough language and vulgarity, full-frontal male and partial female art-model nudity, much sexual banter and innuendo, a couple of minor gay characters, and a stylized strangling. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
